name: Prehistory & Ancient Near East
introduction: Long before anyone kept a house cat, people carved and modelled the wild ones. Big cats flank the seated woman of Çatalhöyük, Mycenaean smiths inlaid wild cats into a bronze dagger blade, and Scythian goldsmiths hammered crouching panthers out of sheet gold. The era runs from the first farming towns to the silver drinking horns of Parthian Iran.

name: Neolithic Anatolia: Çatalhöyük & Hacılar
introduction: Some of the oldest big-cat images anywhere come from two farming towns on the Anatolian plateau. At Çatalhöyük, pairs of leopards in plaster relief faced each other across house walls and a clay woman sits enthroned between two felines; at Hacılar, a seated woman holds a leopard cub.

name: Aegean Bronze Age: Minoan & Mycenaean Art
introduction: Palace frescoes of Minoan Crete and the inlaid weapons of the Mycenaean shaft graves, where cats first appear in Greek lands as hunters stalking birds through river reeds.

name: Scythian & Iranian Animal-Style Metalwork
introduction: Nomad goldsmiths of the Eurasian steppe curled panthers and stags into tight, muscular emblems that archaeologists call the animal style. The Kelermes panther from the Kuban and the gold feline from the Ziwiye hoard in Iran show the idea at its height, and a Parthian silver rhyton carries it into the age of Rome.

name: Ancient Egypt
introduction: In ancient Egyptian civilization, the domestic cat (miu) occupied a unique intersection of domestic affection, practical necessity, and cosmic theology. Revered as manifestations of the goddess Bastet and the solar defender Ra against the serpent Apep, felines were depicted in tomb wall paintings, sacred temple bronzes, and loving domestic reliefs.

name: Middle & New Kingdom Amulets, Jewellery & Faience
introduction: Small, wearable and often blue: these are the cats Egyptians kept on their bodies and dressing tables. A calcite cosmetic jar and faience figurines from the Middle Kingdom lead on to lapis amulets, gold cuff bracelets from the tomb of three foreign wives of Thutmose III, and a faience ring with a mother cat and her kittens.

name: New Kingdom Painting: Tombs, Papyri & Ostraca
introduction: Under the chair, in the marsh, beside the sacred persea tree: New Kingdom painters found room for the cat in the good life and the afterlife alike. The Theban tomb chapels of Nakht and Nebamun show it snacking and hunting, and the village of tomb painters at Deir el-Medina, which gave us the Great Cat of Heliopolis slaying the serpent Apophis, also left limestone flakes with cats waiting on mice.

name: Bastet's Cult: Mummies, Coffins & Amulets
introduction: Cats raised around Bastet's temples were mummified and sold to pilgrims as offerings, and the lucky ones got a carved coffin of their own. This group gathers linen-wrapped mummies, wooden coffins and statuettes, hardstone and faience amulets of the Third Intermediate, Late and Ptolemaic periods, plus one archaizing Saite relief that copies an Old Kingdom marsh scene.

name: Late Period & Ptolemaic Votive Bronzes
introduction: Bastet's popularity peaked after 664 BC, and her worshippers left bronze cats at her temples in their thousands. The Gayer-Anderson cat, with its gold earrings and nose ring, is the star, but the hollow-cast mothers with kittens, the cat-topped sistra and the bronze boxes for cat mummies show how busy the foundries were.

name: Classical Antiquity
introduction: Greek and Etruscan art is full of panthers in Dionysos's train, while the domestic cat sneaks in on an Athenian statue base and only comes into its own on Roman floors, stealing birds. Attic vases, Etruscan tomb paintings and bronzes, Hellenistic gold and Roman floor mosaics follow that shift from the exotic to the household, from the sixth century BC to the Antonine villas.

name: Etruscan & Praenestine Bronzes and Tomb Painting
introduction: Two leopards guard the banquet painted in the Tomb of the Leopards at Tarquinia, and Etruscan bronze casters kept felines about the house. Panther-pawed feet from a Praenestine toilet box and a late incense burner with a cat climbing its stem bring the story down to the Roman conquest.

name: Archaic & Hellenistic Greek Art
introduction: Greek artists liked their felines with a job to do: a cat and a dog squaring up on an Athenian kouros base, panthers prowling the bands of black-figure cups, a panther carrying Dionysos across a pebble floor at Pella. Hellenistic goldsmiths and sculptors carried on with lynx-headed earrings and a marble panther for the god's entourage.

name: Roman Mosaics & Terracottas
introduction: Roman floors are full of cats behaving badly: one pounces on a partridge in the House of the Faun at Pompeii, another eyes a pair of drinking parrots, a third makes off with a bird while ducks look on. Laid in opus vermiculatum, tesserae so small they read like paint, these panels run from the late Republic to the villas of the Antonine emperors, with a terracotta panther head for company.

name: Medieval Europe
introduction: The medieval European imagination viewed the cat with intense ambivalence: cherished by monastic scribes for guarding precious manuscripts from rodents, yet occasionally demonized in theological folklore as nocturnally uncanny. Scribes and illuminators celebrated cats in bestiaries and illuminated margins (drolleries), capturing their absurd acrobatics, mouse-hunting heroics, and humorous subversions.

name: Byzantine Ivories & Gothic Misericords
introduction: Two carvings bracket the Middle Ages. An early Byzantine ivory pyx puts panthers in Dionysos's triumphal procession, and the choir stalls of Great Malvern Priory hide a misericord where the mice hang the cat, the world turned upside down in English oak.

name: Insular Gospel Books
introduction: Monks in Northumbria and Iona worked cats into the knotwork of the gospels. In the Book of Kells, cats sit beside mice nibbling a Eucharistic wafer, and a cat in the Lindisfarne Gospels stretches down the margin of Luke's opening page with eight birds already in its belly.

name: English Bestiaries
introduction: The bestiary explains that the cat is called musio because it hunts mice and cattus because it catches them, and English illuminators illustrated the point with relish. The Aberdeen, Rochester, Harley and Northumberland copies show cats with mice in their jaws, on gold grounds and bare vellum.

name: Gothic Marginalia & Books of Hours
introduction: Around 1300 the margins of prayer books filled up with jokes, and the cat got some of the best lines. A tabby in the Luttrell Psalter clutches a mouse, cats in a Walters Book of Hours bang cymbals and carry a funeral bier, and a North French border of the 1480s tucks one in beside the Pietà.

name: Indigenous Americas & Pre-Columbian Civilizations
introduction: Across Mesoamerica, Central America, and the Andean highlands, pre-Columbian cultures (Olmec, Chavín, Paracas, Nazca, Moche, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú, Maya, and Inca) revered wild felines as sacred embodiments of shamanic transformation, celestial power, and underworld guardianship.

name: Early Horizon Andes: Chavín & Paracas
introduction: The Chavín cult spread a fanged feline face across the Andes, and the Paracas potters of Peru's south coast took it up in incised and resin-painted vessels. A feline mortar from Pacopampa, pampas cats on a square bowl and a cat on a double-spout bottle all belong to the centuries before Nasca.

name: Costa Rica & Panama: Isthmian Gold, Stone & Ceramics
introduction: Between Mesoamerica and the Andes, the chiefdoms of Costa Rica and Panama made the feline an emblem of power. Nicoya carvers shaped feline mace heads, Pataky potters painted jaguar vessels, and Diquís and Veraguas goldsmiths cast double-headed cats and jaguars in gold by the lost-wax method.

name: Moche, Nasca, Wari & the Northern Andes
introduction: After Chavín the Andes split into regional styles, each with its own idea of a cat. Moche potters on the north coast modelled them in the round and cast them in copper, Nasca lapidaries inlaid them in shell, a Wari carver polished one in stone with turquoise, and resist-painted bowls from the Colombian highlands give the jaguar the last word.

name: Mesoamerica: Maya & Aztec
introduction: In Mesoamerica the jaguar belonged to rulers and warriors: Maya kings sat on jaguar-pelt thrones, and elite Aztec soldiers fought as jaguar warriors. A Classic Maya jade pendant and an Aztec stone feline from Central Mexico stand at the two ends of that tradition.

name: East, South & Southeast Asia
introduction: Chinese court painters punned on cats and butterflies to wish someone a long life, Joseon painters laid down their fur a hair at a time, and Edo printmakers dressed them as kabuki actors. This era gathers China, Korea, Japan, India and Southeast Asia from the Song dynasty to Taishō Japan, from Khmer stoneware to Kalighat bazaar paintings.

name: Song & Ming Painting
introduction: Song painters set the standard for cats on silk: Yi Yuanji was famed for studying animals in the wild, and an anonymous Song album leaf shows a kitten with every hair in place. The Ming Xuande Emperor painted cats himself, Shen Zhou sketched one from life for his album, and late Ming court artists kept the Song manner going.

name: South & Southeast Asia: Khmer to Kalighat
introduction: A Khmer stoneware lime pot shaped like a cat, a Siamese treatise on lucky and unlucky cats, paintings sold to pilgrims outside the Kalighat temple in Kolkata: South and Southeast Asian cats turn up in workshops, temples and bazaars rather than courts. A Raj-era photograph of a hunted leopard adds the colonial view.

name: Joseon Dynasty Korean Painting
introduction: Joseon painters, led by Byeon Sang-byeok, nicknamed 'Byeon the Cat', and Kim Hong-do, painted cats in gardens with the fur laid down a hair at a time. The sparrows, butterflies and chrysanthemums around them carry wishes for long life and joy.

name: Edo Carving, Metalwork & Ceramics
introduction: Japan's most famous cat sleeps over a gateway at the Nikkō Tōshō-gū, carved for the 1636 rebuilding and credited to Hidari Jingorō. Edo craftsmen also put cats on sword guards and knife handles, carved them as netsuke toggles, fired them in Hizen porcelain and set stone guardian cats before a Kotohira shrine.

name: Qing Painting, Prints & Porcelain
introduction: Qing cats come in every register. Bada Shanren gave his cat a sulky inked eye on a rock, Suzhou printshops sold cheerful colour woodblocks of cats for the wall, Jingdezhen fired porcelain cats to sit by the bed, and the Shanghai painter Xugu set one under a butterfly, the old pun on a long life.

name: Edo & Meiji Brush Painting: Haiga, Shijō & Maruyama
introduction: Not every Edo cat lived in a print. A Kyoto monk-poet brushed his dreaming cat in ink beside a comic verse, Matsumura Goshun, founder of the Shijō school, parodied a famous priest with a cat and a poem, and Meiji painters such as Kawabata Gyokushō, Ōide Tōkō and the Kanō-trained Kawanabe Kyōsai carried that observant brushwork into the 1880s and 90s.

name: Ukiyo-e: Beauties, Monsters & Meiji Prints
introduction: Beyond the Utagawa studios, the floating world drew cats in several moods. Tsukioka Settei and Kitagawa Utamaro set them beside fashionable women, Toriyama Sekien catalogued the fork-tailed nekomata in his illustrated book of monsters, and Kobayashi Kiyochika lit a cat by lantern light in the new Meiji print style.

name: Utagawa School: Kuniyoshi, Kunisada & Hiroshige
introduction: Utagawa Kuniyoshi kept a houseful of cats and drew them into everything: as kabuki actors, as walking proverbs, as the fifty-three stations of the Tōkaidō and as the monster cat of Okabe. Fellow Utagawa artists Kunisada and Hiroshige, and his pupil Yoshitoyo, slipped cats into actor triptychs, landscapes and news sheets.

name: Nihonga & Meiji–Taishō Book Design
introduction: Nihonga, 'Japanese-style painting', set mineral pigments and ink on silk against the European oil painting arriving in Meiji Japan. Hishida Shunsō, a pioneer of the outline-free 'hazy style', set a black cat on an oak trunk, Takeuchi Seihō painted a tabby with Kyoto-school precision, and Hashiguchi Goyō, trained in the same circles, dressed Natsume Sōseki's I Am a Cat for its 1905 first edition.

name: The Islamic World
introduction: By tradition, the Prophet's companion Abu Hurayra owes his name, 'father of the kitten', to a cat he carried in his sleeve, and cats have padded through Islamic art ever since. This era runs from Seljuq bronzes and lustre bowls through illustrated fable books and Mughal hunting pictures, with their trained cheetahs, to the large oil portraits of Zand and Qajar Iran.

name: Seljuq Bronzes & Ceramics
introduction: Under the Seljuqs, workshops in Khurasan cast bronze incense burners shaped like big cats, their bodies pierced so the smoke would curl out. Iranian potters painted leopards in lustre and moulded hunters riding out with cheetahs perched behind them in turquoise-glazed stonepaste.

name: Kalila wa Dimna & Anwar-i Suhaili
introduction: Kalila wa Dimna, the Arabic version of the Indian Panchatantra, is full of animals scheming at court, and its Persian retelling, the Anwar-i Suhaili ('Lights of Canopus'), kept painters busy for centuries. Here a trapped cat bargains with a mouse, a leopard carries a lion's orders, and a hunter takes aim at another leopard.

name: Safavid, Zand & Qajar Iran
introduction: Safavid weavers worked cheetahs pouncing on deer into court silks, and the oil painters of Zand Shiraz and Qajar Tehran later gave the cat a place beside their large, glossy portraits of court women. A lady with a cat in her arms became a small Qajar specialty.

name: Mughal Court Painting
introduction: Akbar's painters showed the emperor hunting blackbuck with trained cheetahs, hooded and carried to the field on carts, and Prince Salim's artists at Allahabad and in later albums kept up the hunting theme. By the eighteenth century the mood had softened: a late Mughal princess chases a cat to save her parrot.

name: The Renaissance
introduction: The European Renaissance re-engaged with direct empirical observation and humanistic symbolism, casting cats in complex dual roles. While Leonardo da Vinci dissected the mechanical elegance of feline muscles and movement, painters like Lotto, Veronese, and Dürer wove cats into sacred scenes as symbols of domestic intimacy, sensory distraction, or theological tension.

name: Early & High Renaissance: Florence, Rome & Milan
introduction: Leonardo filled sheets with cats twisting, sleeping and squabbling while he worked out a Madonna with a cat, and his Milanese followers took the idea up. In Florentine, Roman and Sienese frescoes a cat often sits under the table at the Last Supper or plays by Penelope's loom, a household detail that grounds the story.

name: Venetian Renaissance
introduction: Venetian painters loved a crowded table, and somebody always let the cat in. Veronese put cats under his feasts at Cana and in the House of Levi, Tintoretto and Bassano set them beside the Last Supper, Antonello's Saint Jerome shares his study with one, and in Lotto's Recanati Annunciation a tabby bolts as the angel lands.

name: German Renaissance: Dürer, Baldung & the Little Masters
introduction: Dürer's 1504 Adam and Eve puts a cat and a mouse at the couple's feet, coded to the four temperaments, and the German Renaissance never quite let the cat go. Baldung's cats keep company with witches and allegories, Aldegrever's attends Gluttony, and the 1491 Hortus Sanitatis describes the cat for physicians.

name: Early Netherlandish & Antwerp Renaissance
introduction: From Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, where a cat walks off with its prey in Eden, to Bruegel's man belling the cat in Netherlandish Proverbs, Low Countries artists used cats to point a moral. Woodcuts, silver-stained glass roundels and engravings from Leiden, Amsterdam and Antwerp spread the same proverbs and warnings to a wider public.

name: Barocci & the Late Renaissance
introduction: Federico Barocci of Urbino painted the Madonna of the Cat and kept returning to sleeping cats, at the foot of his Annunciation and in his etching of it. Around him, Vincenzo Campi's Cremona kitchens, Roman ornament prints, Sienese grotesque studies and Della Porta's book on human physiognomy show the cat at work in late sixteenth-century Italy.

name: Northern Mannerist Prints
introduction: Late sixteenth-century engravers in Antwerp, Haarlem, Cologne, Dresden and Frankfurt made the cat a stock character of the moral print: the scratched playmate of Childhood, the troublemaker of the bad household, the howling keyboard of a cat clavichord. Goltzius's Sight and Galle's hunting plates after Stradanus add it to the Five Senses and the chase.

name: The Baroque & Dutch Golden Age
introduction: Genre painting and still life took over the seventeenth century, and the cat moved into the kitchen. Dutch and Flemish painters cast it as fish thief and reluctant dance pupil, French etchers sent it out with Callot's beggars, and in Bologna Annibale Carracci let two children tease one with a crayfish.

name: Italian & Spanish Baroque
introduction: Annibale Carracci's two children teasing a cat with a crayfish announced a new, unvarnished naturalism in Bologna. A century of Italian painters followed with cats in kitchens, lacemakers' rooms and wedding feasts, and in Velázquez's Las Hilanderas a cat dozes among the spinners of the royal weaving works.

name: Dutch Golden Age Prints
introduction: Cornelis Visscher's Large Cat, dozing on a ledge while a mouse creeps out behind it, is the best-known cat in Dutch printmaking. Rembrandt slipped a cat into his etched Holy Family, and Amsterdam publishers kept the presses busy with cat concerts, proverbs and fable prints in etching and mezzotint.

name: Dutch Still Life & Allegory
introduction: Dutch still-life painters let cats into the composition mainly to wreck it. Abraham Mignon's cat sends a vase of flowers flying, Jan Baptist Weenix's cat and dog square up over hunting spoils, and an anonymous allegory of 1612 brings one into its plea for religious peace.

name: Antwerp Still Life, Singerie & Peasant Genre
introduction: In Antwerp, Clara Peeters and Frans Snyders set cats loose on fish and larders, Jan van Kessel painted cat concerts on copper, and the Teniers family ran barbershops staffed by monkeys and cats, the comic genre called singerie. Wenceslaus Hollar, in exile in the city, etched a cat's head small enough to hold in the palm.

name: French Baroque: Callot, Bosse & the Le Nain
introduction: Jacques Callot in Lorraine etched a beggar woman with her cats and a cat eyeing a caged bird, and Abraham Bosse let a cat doze beside his Foolish Virgins. The Le Nain brothers painted peasant families at home with the household cat, everyone serious and unhurried.

name: Haarlem, Dordrecht & Rotterdam Genre
introduction: In Haarlem, Judith Leyster painted children teasing a cat with an eel; in Dordrecht, Rembrandt's pupils Nicolaes Maes and Samuel van Hoogstraten put cats in quiet interiors where maids nap and ladies wilt. Cornelis Saftleven's Rotterdam stables and Hendrik Potuyl's courtyards have cats on duty too, usually the only ones paying attention.

name: Leiden Fine Painters & Jan Steen
introduction: Leiden produced two kinds of genre painter: the fijnschilders ('fine painters') around Gerard Dou, who polished every whisker, and Jan Steen, who let the household run riot. Steen's children teach a cat to dance and to read, Metsu's old woman shares her breakfast with one, and Dou's cat crouches on a studio ledge.

name: The Eighteenth Century
introduction: The Enlightenment and Rococo eras transformed the domestic cat into an emblem of bourgeois refinement, feminine intimacy, and biting social satire. From Chardin's visceral still lifes and Perronneau's luminous pastels to Hogarth's cautionary London moralities and Goya's nocturnal tensions, cats reflected the anxieties and luxuries of the age.

name: Rococo & Enlightenment Painting
introduction: Chardin and Desportes caught the bristling ferocity of cats raiding the kitchen, while Boucher, Perronneau, Fragonard and Marguerite Gérard made the kitten an emblem of private, comfortable life. Court painters such as Bacciarelli in Warsaw carried the same taste across Europe.

name: Porcelain & Pottery Figures: Meissen to Staffordshire
introduction: Once the Meissen factory, founded in 1710, had cracked the secret of hard-paste porcelain, cats arrived on mantelpieces across Europe. Meissen modellers made them into snuffboxes and harlequins' companions, Nymphenburg added a girl with her cat, and English makers in London, Derby and Staffordshire answered with soft-paste toys, enamels, salt-glazed stoneware and creamware cats.

name: British Georgian Painting & Satire
introduction: Hogarth used a cat to make a point: one stares hungrily at the Graham children's caged goldfinch, another is tormented in the First Stage of Cruelty. Gainsborough and Reynolds preferred the cat as a sitter's pet, and William Blake painted Thomas Gray's drowned cat among his watercolour illustrations to Gray's poems.

name: Goya & the Spanish Enlightenment
introduction: Goya's cats moved with his career. They spit at each other on a wall in a cartoon for the royal weaving works, stare at a magpie in the portrait of little Manuel Osorio, and join the creatures of the night in The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters.

name: The Nineteenth Century
introduction: The nineteenth century turned the cat into a career. Gottfried Mind's kittens went round the German-speaking world in lithograph, Ronner-Knip in Brussels and Julius 'Katzen-Adam' in Munich painted little else, Manet put a black cat at the foot of Olympia's bed, and Steinlen made one the mascot of a Montmartre cabaret. Across the Atlantic, Currier & Ives sold kitten prints to American parlours.

name: Gottfried Mind & Swiss Biedermeier Prints
introduction: Gottfried Mind of Bern earned the nickname 'Raphael of Cats' with watercolours of mother cats and kittens drawn from his own pets. After his death in 1814, lithographers such as Joseph Brodtmann turned his studies into prints for a German-speaking public that could not get enough of them.

name: American Folk Portraits & Needlework
introduction: Itinerant portraitists like Ammi Phillips painted children with their cats against plain, flat grounds, and Edward Hicks tucked a leopard among the lambs of his Peaceable Kingdom. At home, women in Vermont and New York stitched cats into embroidered carpets, appliqué and crazy quilts.

name: Danish Golden Age & Dutch Drawing from Life
introduction: Copenhagen's painters drew what was in front of them, and often that was the household cat. Købke, Skovgaard and Lundbye sketched cats asleep in pen and pencil, Jerichau modelled two kittens with a ball, and David Jacobsen took the habit to Paris; in Amsterdam the amateur Jean Bernard was doing the same.

name: French Romanticism & Realism
introduction: Géricault studied a dead cat as coolly as a dead horse, Daumier and Millet put cats into Paris garrets and farm kitchens, and Courbet let one play on the floor of his studio allegory. Manet then made the cat a provocation, raising its tail at the foot of Olympia's bed and drawing its rooftop rendezvous for Champfleury's book Les Chats.

name: Book & Fable Illustration
introduction: Lithography and cheap wood engraving put pictures in every book, and cats came along. Ackermann's lithographers staged a cat concert in Regency London, Doré's Puss in Boots swaggers through Perrault, Lambert's cats act out La Fontaine for Hetzel's editions, and Beardsley drew Poe's Black Cat sitting on the corpse.

name: Currier & Ives & American Popular Prints
introduction: Nathaniel Currier's New York shop, later Currier & Ives, sold hand-coloured lithographs cheap enough for any parlour wall, and kittens were steady sellers. Chromolithographs after European painters such as Ronner-Knip brought the salon cat to the same customers.

name: American Genre & Gilded Age Painting
introduction: American painters brought cats into the parlour pictures their clients wanted: William Morris Hunt and Eastman Johnson in the 1850s, John Henry Dolph, New York's cat painter, in the Gilded Age. Cecilia Beaux closes the century with a Philadelphia portrait of a man and his cat.

name: Victorian Narrative & Animal Painting
introduction: Victorian painters knew a cat could sell a picture. Charles Burton Barber painted Queen Victoria's pets, Horatio Henry Couldery specialised in kittens with fishbowls and unexpected guests, Millais floated a cat in a cradle down A Flood, and Holman Hunt put one under the table of The Awakening Conscience, toying with a bird.

name: Victorian Decorative Arts & Historicism
introduction: Industry made the cat a product. Minton majolica, Barbedienne enamelled bronze, Pittsburgh pressed glass, Parian porcelain, Paterson woven silk pictures and cold-painted Vienna bronzes all put cats on nineteenth-century shelves, and the Gothic Revival even restored one to a choir stall at Great Malvern.

name: Ronner-Knip & Continental Academic Cat Painting
introduction: Henriëtte Ronner-Knip painted cats in Brussels for half a century, working from a glass-fronted box so her kittens could not wander off, and her pictures sold across Europe and America. Julius Adam in Munich, Carl Reichert in Graz and the animal painters of the Paris Salon made cat painting a specialty of its own.

name: Plein-Air Naturalism & National Realisms
introduction: Across Europe in the later nineteenth century, painters left the studio for the farmyard and the parlour as they really looked. Bruno Liljefors watched cats hunt in Swedish gardens and meadows, Carl Larsson painted his daughter Brita at Sundborn with a cat and a sandwich, Walter Osborne brought Bastien-Lepage's naturalism to Ireland, and Yaroshenko, Grigorescu and Chierici painted the cats of Russia, Romania and Italy.

name: Impressionism
introduction: Impressionists painted cats where they actually were, in laps and among the flowers. Renoir put them in the arms of Julie Manet and of a young woman, Manet painted his wife with a cat on her knee, Morisot drew a little girl with a grey one, and in Amsterdam Breitner sketched a cat asleep.

name: Muybridge & Chronophotography
introduction: In Philadelphia in the mid-1880s Eadweard Muybridge lined up batteries of cameras against a gridded backdrop and photographed people and animals in motion, a cat among them. The plates of Animal Locomotion (1887) showed what the eye alone could not: exactly where a galloping cat puts its feet.

name: Post-Impressionism, Nabis & Symbolism
introduction: Van Gogh painted a black cat slipping across Daubigny's garden in his last weeks at Auvers, and Bonnard's White Cat arches into an impossible stretch. Vallotton's flat woodcuts, Toulouse-Lautrec's cabaret posters, Ślewiński's Pont-Aven sleeper and Redon's cat on a roof show how many ways the 1890s found to simplify one.

name: Le Chat Noir & Montmartre
introduction: Rodolphe Salis opened the Chat Noir cabaret in 1881, and its weekly journal needed pictures. Steinlen supplied wordless cat comic strips, painted the Apotheosis of the Cats for the cabaret, and in 1896 drew the black cat on the poster for the troupe's tour.

name: Louis Wain & the Victorian Cat Fancy
introduction: Louis Wain began by drawing real cats at real shows, reporting from the Crystal Palace and Brighton for the illustrated press, and only gradually stood them on their hind legs. By the late 1890s his cats threw bachelor parties and paraded in Hyde Park, and Britain could not get enough of them.

name: Art Nouveau Posters, Prints & Medals
introduction: Steinlen spent the late 1890s turning his own cats into posters, album covers, lithographs and drypoints for a Paris that collected them avidly. Edward Penfield's calendar covers carried the poster craze to America, and the medallist Sylla Eustache struck a portrait plaquette of a cat named Kiribi.

name: Early Twentieth Century
introduction: The opening decades of the twentieth century dismantled classical illusionism. Franz Marc turned cats into blocks of pure colour, Gwen John gave them quiet Parisian interiors, Paul Klee made them a line, and René Lalique poured them into glass. Cameras and film arrived too, and the cat promptly stole the scene.

name: Edwardian Book Illustration
introduction: The golden age of British illustration had plenty of cats. Beatrix Potter gave Miss Moppet and Tom Kitten their own little books in 1906 and 1907, Arthur Rackham sketched a parrot and a cat for a children's poem, and Byam Shaw drew Poe's Black Cat.

name: Academic Cat Painting after 1900
introduction: The salon cat outlived the century. Henriëtte Ronner-Knip, past eighty, was still painting kitten studies in Brussels around 1904, Julius 'Katzen-Adam' kept turning out baskets of kittens in Munich, and Charles van den Eycken built a Belgian career on cats meddling with paintboxes and snails.

name: Młoda Polska (Young Poland)
introduction: Młoda Polska (Young Poland) was a Polish modernist movement (c. 1890–1918) synthesising Symbolism, Art Nouveau, and early modernism across literature, music, and the visual arts.

name: Late Impressionism & Nabi Intimism
introduction: Impressionism did not stop in 1900. Mary Cassatt kept painting children and cats in Paris until her eyesight failed, and Bonnard set a woman and her cat at the table in the warm, close interiors the Nabis called intimist.

name: Steinlen after 1900
introduction: Steinlen kept drawing cats long after the Chat Noir closed in 1897: posters for a veterinary clinic and an animal artists' show, seasonal prints of a cat on a cushion and on a balustrade, a small sculpture, and etched pairs of cats asleep or at rest made in 1914.

name: Louis Wain's Edwardian Cats
introduction: In the 1900s Louis Wain was the best-known cat artist in Britain: his upright, grinning cats filled annuals, magazines and Raphael Tuck postcards, went to the theatre, crashed motorcars and held Christmas balls in Catville. Poor contracts and a spell in New York left him broke all the same.

name: British Etching & Wood-Engraving Revival
introduction: Printmaking became a fine art again in Edwardian and interwar Britain, and its artists kept cats. William Strang etched Montaigne with his, C. R. W. Nevinson made one in aquatint, and John Nash and Eileen Mayo cut cats into wood.

name: Nordic & Dutch Painting and Illustration
introduction: Danish and Swedish painters of the new century kept the cat in its old place by the stove: Carl Holsøe in a Copenhagen interior of grey light, Ludvig Find and the Funen painters in country houses, Niels Skovgaard in storybooks, Liljefors still in his meadows. In The Hague, Julie de Graag drew her cat Poes beside the dog Max and the tortoise Akbar.

name: Japonisme Woodcut & Shin-hanga
introduction: Japanese woodblock prints taught the West to cut colour into wood, and the lesson ran both ways. Helen Hyde worked in Tokyo with Japanese carvers and printers, Ethel Mars cut colour woodcuts in Paris, and Takahashi Shōtei designed a hissing black cat for the shin-hanga ('new prints') publishers of Tokyo.

name: Early Photography & Film
introduction: A kitten dosed with a spoon in a 1903 Brighton film, an actress posing with her cat for Arnold Genthe, an airship crew's mascot: the camera learned early that cats will happily star in front of it. Edward Steichen's print of 1902 gave the cat the soft focus of Pictorialism.

name: École de Paris
introduction: École de Paris names the crowd of French and émigré artists who made Paris the centre of modern art between 1900 and 1940. Their cats are just as cosmopolitan: Chagall's human-faced cat on the windowsill, Valadon's Raminou, Tanaka Yasushi's cat among flowers, Makowski's children with theirs, Balthus as the King of Cats, and Picasso's cat with a bird in its jaws.

name: Russian & Polish Genre Painting
introduction: Figurative painting held its ground against the avant-garde in Russia and Poland. Kustodiev's merchant's wife takes tea while her cat rubs against her shoulder, and Polish painters such as Wasilkowski, Ejsmond and Bakałowicz kept putting cats into salon pictures for a public that liked them.

name: Paris Animaliers & Art Deco Glass
introduction: Paris made the cat sleek. Rembrandt Bugatti modelled a walking panther, Lalique wound cats around a choker and later pressed them into frosted glass, George Barbier drew a lady and her panther for the fashion press, and Pompon smoothed his panther into a single polished curve.

name: Modern Chinese Painting
introduction: Early twentieth-century Chinese painting that reformed traditional ink practice through Western academic realism, championed by Xu Beihong and his contemporaries.

name: Gwen John's Paris Cats
introduction: Living alone in Paris and modelling for Rodin, Gwen John drew her tortoiseshell cat over and over: washing, sleeping, curled into a ball. The drawings are small, quick and exact, and when the cat went missing she searched the streets for it.

name: Fauvism, Die Brücke & German Modernism
introduction: Outside Marc's circle the cat took on modernism's other accents. Matisse sat his daughter Marguerite with a black cat in flat colour, Kirchner painted himself with a cat in Davos, Rik Wouters drew his cat Flip in wartime exile, Paula Modersohn-Becker put a girl and a cat in a birch wood, and Klee balanced a bird on a cat's forehead.

name: Der Blaue Reiter & Munich Expressionism
introduction: Franz Marc thought animals saw the world more purely than people did, and he painted cats in red, yellow and blue to prove it. With Kandinsky he launched the Blaue Reiter in Munich in 1911, and his friend August Macke painted a cat sunning itself on a garden bench.

name: Louis Wain: Kaleidoscopic & Late Hospital Works
introduction: During his later years confined to Springfield, Bethlem Royal, and Napsbury hospitals, Louis Wain transformed his beloved comic felines into vibrating astral entities. Laying down saturated gouache in electrifying geometric fractals, Turkish-carpet spirals, and radiant halos, Wain dissolved the boundary between British illustration and visionary outsider modernism.

name: Witkacy & Polish Interwar Graphic Art
introduction: Stanisław Ignacy Witkiewicz, Witkacy, ran his portraiture as a business, the S. I. Witkiewicz Portrait Painting Firm, with printed rules and price categories, and he noted on his pastels which stimulants he had taken. Cats crept into his grotesques too, sick kittens and all, while Wiktoria Goryńska of the Ryt society cut a cat in wood.

name: WPA Federal Art Project
introduction: From 1935 the Works Progress Administration paid American artists to make art, and New York printmakers and Chicago painters handed in cats. Chuzo Tamotzu's lithograph, Mabel Wellington Jack's sleeping kitten and Gertrude Abercrombie's dreamlike White Cat all date from those relief years.

name: Mid-Twentieth Century & Modernism
introduction: Surrealists and postwar painters read the cat as a creature of psychic mystery and unease. On the same decades' ships and battlefields, real cats worked as mascots and mouse-hunters, and animators, jewellers and Pop pioneers were already drawing them for the mass market.

name: Wartime & Post-War Figuration
introduction: Picasso sat Dora Maar in a chair with a small cat at her shoulder in 1941 and modelled a cat in bronze during the Occupation. After the war Balthus painted a cat-headed diner with a rainbow of fish, Lucian Freud painted a young woman holding a kitten by the neck, and Giacometti cast a cat as thin as one of his walking men.

name: Late Surrealism: Mexico & New York
introduction: Surrealism's second life after 1940 happened largely in exile and in the Americas. Frida Kahlo set a black cat at her shoulder in the Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, Remedios Varo let a cat's fury spark through a quiet room, and Philippe Halsman and Salvador Dalí threw cats and a bucket of water through the air for Dalí Atomicus.

name: Ship Cats & Wartime Mascots
introduction: Navies kept cats for the mice and for morale. Peebles of HMS Western Isles, Oscar, the 'Unsinkable Sam' of naval legend said to have survived the Bismarck, and Simon of HMS Amethyst, awarded the Dickin Medal, served in photographs, pastel portraits and stories.

name: British Illustration & Photography
introduction: Paper rationing did not stop British illustrators. Rolf Brandt drew Poe's Black Cat in Neo-Romantic gloom, Eileen Mayo engraved a cat in a cherry tree, and Kathleen Hale's Orlando the Marmalade Cat went to sea on an ocean liner's menu cards. Thurston Hopkins photographed London for Picture Post, and studio photographers posed cats for the salon.

name: Animation, Jewellery & Early Warhol
introduction: Figaro the kitten stole scenes in Disney's Pinocchio, Van Cleef & Arpels set a mischievous cat in gold for its Paris boutique, and in 1954 the young Andy Warhol printed 25 Cats Name Sam and One Blue Pussy, the missing 'd' courtesy of his mother's hand lettering.

name: Late Twentieth Century & Contemporary Art
introduction: After 1960 the cat goes public: on plinths on Highgate Hill and in Gough Square, scissor-cut in Chinese villages, tongue out on Polish circus posters. Painters and printmakers keep it close too, from Hockney's Percy to Lola Dupré's photocollage portraits.

name: Poster Art: Polish School, OSPAAAL & Psychedelia
introduction: Posters were where the 1960s and 70s argued in public. Hubert Hilscher's Cyrk posters for the Polish state circus, Alfredo Rostgaard's black panther for Cuba's OSPAAAL, a San Francisco Cheshire Cat in full psychedelic colour and Dewynters' yellow-eyed poster for Cats all use the feline to stop you in the street.

name: Industrial Design: Tiles, Tableware & Toys
introduction: Mass production loved a cat motif. Hornsea Pottery ran a line of cats around a beaker, Christina Sheppard scratched a cat in a window through the glaze of a tile, and Chinese factories lithographed tinplate cats that bat a ball when wound up.

name: Studio Printmaking: Woodcut, Lithograph & Etching
introduction: Artist-printmakers after 1960 cut, drew and bit their own cats. Sekino Jun'ichirō's sōsaku hanga ('creative prints') woodblock, Jacques Hnizdovsky's tabby in black-and-white woodcut, Tatyana Kozmina's village lithograph and Toshihiko Ikeda's etched old cat all keep the artist's own hand in the print.

name: Folk Crafts & Self-Taught Art
introduction: Some of the liveliest cats after 1960 came from outside the art schools. Chinese papercutters in Henan and Shaanxi snipped cats from paper, a Prague puppet maker gave three can-can cats their feathers, James Lloyd, a farmhand turned painter, built his cat out of tiny dots, and Nellie Mae Rowe drew a big cat in Georgia.

name: British Figurative Art & Printmaking
introduction: British artists kept faith with the figure after Pop. Hockney's white cat Percy sits on Ossie Clark's knee, Elisabeth Frink and Bryan Organ drew wild cats, lynx and cheetahs for lithographs, Barry Flanagan, better known for hares, etched a cat, and Peter Till drew the boardroom 'fat cats' of the 1990s.

name: Danish Late Modernism
introduction: Richard Mortensen spent his career on abstraction and still drew cats, a black one lying flat and a cat-mule of his own invention. Arne Haugen Sørensen of the Grønningen group painted birds and stripy cats in bright figurative colour.

name: Public Monuments
introduction: Cities like to commemorate a famous cat. Dick Whittington's companion sits on Highgate Hill, Dr Johnson's Hodge has his oyster shells in Gough Square, and the Cat of Kazan, hero of Russian lubok prints, has a statue of its own.

name: Photography & Photocollage
introduction: Photographers after 1960 took the cat from the salon to the street and back. Charles Wormald put one in a goldfish bowl for the Royal Photographic Society crowd, Roger Ballen staged a cat catcher in his unsettling South African Outland, and Lola Dupré cuts photographs into hand-made collage portraits of cats.
